Dr. '''Rudolf Maria "Ruud" Tromp''' (born 3 September 1954, [[Alkmaar]])<ref name=APS>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Tromp&first_nm=Rudolf&year=2003|title=2003 Davisson-Germer Prize in Atomic or Surface Physics Recipient|website=[[American Physical Society]]|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref> is a [[Dutch people|Dutch]] American scientist at [[IBM Research]] Division, [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] and a Physics Professor at [[Leiden University]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/staffmembers/ruud-tromp|title=Ruud Tromp {{!}} Professor of Physics of surfaces and materials|website=[[Leiden University]]|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>

==Education==
He attended Petrus Canisius College, The Lyceum ([[Alkmaar]]).
*1982 Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of Utrecht]] (The [[Netherlands]])
*1982, completed a thesis on medium-energy ion scattering (MEIS) studies of the structure of silicon surfaces.

==Biography==
In 1983 he joined IBM at the Thomas J. Watson Research Center, where his [[scanning tunneling microscopy]] studies revealed the Si(001) dimer structure for the first time, as well as the spatial distribution of the Si(111) (7 × 7) electronic surface states and their relation to the underlying atomic structure. Using MEIS, he co-invented “surfactant-mediated epitaxial growth,” a technique that allows much-improved control over the morphology of epitaxial films and superlattices.

More recently, his studies have focused on the dynamics of surface and interface processes such as [[phase transition]]s, [[chemisorption]] and etching, [[Epitaxy|epitaxial growth]], and aspects of nanotechnology. Ultrahigh-vacuum transmission electron microscopy and [[low-energy electron microscopy]] allow detailed, real-time, in situ observations of such processes with high spatial resolution. Using those techniques, the studies have shed new light on the thermodynamics of epitaxial growth, the dynamic evolution of the surface morphology of epitaxial films, the self-assembly of quantum dots, the spatiotemporal character of first- and second-order phase transitions at surfaces, etc. 
He has also developed a novel Low Energy Electron Microscopy instrument, including energy filtering and aberration correction.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tromp|first1=R. M.|last2=Hannon|first2=J. B.|display-authors=etal|date=June 2010|title=A new aberration-corrected, energy-filtered LEEM/PEEM instrument. I. Principles and design|journal=[[Ultramicroscopy]]|volume=110|issue=7|pages=852–861|doi=10.1016/j.ultramic.2010.03.005|pmid=20395048}}</ref>

==Awards==
* 1981: [[Wayne B. Nottingham Prize]] of the [[Physical Electronics Conference]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.princeton.edu/~chemdept/PEC/Nottingham.html|title=Past Winners of the Nottingham Prize|website=[[Princeton University]]|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>
* 1995: Materials Research [[Honor Society|Society Medal]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mrs.org/medal|title=MRS Medal Recipients|website=[[Materials Research Society]]|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>
* 2003: American Physical Society [[Davisson-Germer Prize in Atomic or Surface Physics|Davisson-Germer Prize]]<ref name=APS/>
* 2004: [[American Vacuum Society]] [[Medard W. Welch Award]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.avs.org/popup.aspx?FileName=medard|title=Medard W. Welch Award|website=[[American Vacuum Society]]|access-date=12 December 2019|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050403230528/http://www.avs.org/popup.aspx?FileName=medard|archive-date=3 April 2005}}</ref>
* 2009: [[Materials Research Society]] (MRS) Fellow<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mrs.org/mrs-fellows-list|title=List of MRS Fellows|website=Materials Research Society|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>
* Four IBM Outstanding Innovation and Technical Achievement Awards.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Awardee-Interviews/Interviews/Rudolf-Tromp/Bio|title=Medard W. Welch Award|website=American Vacuum Society|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>
* 2020: [[National Academy of Engineering]] Member 
Dr. Tromp is a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite press release|url=https://www-03.ibm.com/press/us/en/pressrelease/22074.wss|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304061653/http://www-03.ibm.com/press/us/en/pressrelease/22074.wss|url-status=dead|archive-date=4 March 2016|title=Rudolf Tromp to receive the Davisson-Germer Prize {{!}} Recognized for his understanding of semiconductor surfaces and interfaces|date=3 March 2003|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref> the [[American Vacuum Society]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society|title=Society Honors|website=American Vacuum Society|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref> the [[Materials Research Society]] and of the [[Boehmische Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bnl.gov/ecrs2017/files/pdf/ECRS2017_Program.pdf|title=Morning Keynote Speaker - Dr. Rudolf Tromp|website=[[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.eetimes.com/growth-envisioned-for-semiconducting-crystals/|title=Growth envisioned for semiconducting crystals|magazine=[[EE Times]]|date=17 March 2003|author=R. Colin Johnson|access-date=12 December 2019}}</ref>
